reading.identification: A single bay of the row of tiny lean-to booth houses (the historic tripe-sellers' 'penshuisjes') built against the Groentenmarkt flank of Ghent's late-Gothic Groot Vleeshuis, c. 1407-19: a 4.3 m wide, 2.6 m deep limestone shop house, currently enclosed within the hall's restoration hoarding.
reading.notes:
Material: the wall inside the outline is clearly weathered coursed limestone (Tournai/Balegem), not brick — visible at full resolution in set B image 0 above the hoarding. The enum has no stone class; 'concrete' is the correct ITU-R P.2040 stand-in for stone masonry at 28 GHz (eps_r ~5-7), whereas 'marble' should be reserved for polished cladding. Trim is the same lithology as the wall (stone dressings, sills, jambs), so it takes the same class. roughness_mm 9 carries the 1-10 cm regime — eroded rubble coursing and deeply recessed/washed-out mortar joints — as a scattering parameter, NOT as mesh; do not tessellate the joints.

Evidence discipline: only material is marked seen. The stone-mullioned lights, moulded sills and horizontal drip courses legible in set B belong to the parent hall's flank and roof dormers above this polygon, not to the booth itself, whose entire frontage is behind the white picket hoarding. Set A (Google 3D tiles) is a melted mush here and resolves nothing — it corroborates only that the square is enclosed and that spiky gabled forms sit on the far side.

Height: height_source is 'no-data', so 9.0 m is a fallback, not a measurement. I have not overridden it. Storey heights (3.0 + 2.6 = 5.6 m of wall) leave ~3.4 m of steeply-raking shed roof abutting the hall's flank, which is what the low slate lean-tos at the base of the wall in image 0 actually look like. Do not render 9 m of vertical wall on a 2.6 m deep footprint — it would read as a visible primitive from any rotated camera.

Roof marked inferred deliberately: set B is the weak evidence for roof form per the brief, and although low lean-to slate planes are visible at the wall base I cannot certify which annexe polygon they belong to. Shed with the high edge against the hall (south/inboard) and the eaves to the square; ridge line parallel to the frontage.

Cornice false is a consequence of the abutment — a lean-to against a taller hall gets a stone coping and eaves course, not a returned cornice. Sills and string courses are true on the prior for this fabric and are corroborated by the surrounding hall stonework. Balconies false with high confidence: nothing in this typology or on this square carries one.

Detail budget: spend it on the ground floor and the openings — the timber stall front, the deep stone reveals (~0.4-0.5 m walls), the sill and lintel wedges, and the eaves/coping edge. These are the >10 cm features that set street-level field on a 0.1 m setback. The upper wall and the roof plane deserve very little.

Scene context, important: fronting_street is pedestrian with car_access 'none' and paving_stones. Do NOT place parked or moving vehicles on Groentenmarkt. Populate instead with market stalls, cafe terrace tables and chairs, bins, bollards and dense bike parking, which is what this square actually carries. The yellow scaffolding, the tower crane and the white picket hoarding in both photographs are a temporary works state and must not be modelled as permanent fabric.
